# Why does my car jerk and jump when I stop?

Your 2012 Buick Regal is exhibiting classic symptoms of a mismatch between engine speed and transmission input, often described as "jerking" or "jumping." This behavior during deceleration and acceleration typically points to a vacuum leak, a slipping torque converter, or a failing throttle body idle control. When you approach a stop sign, the car's logic attempts to maintain idle RPMs while your foot eases off the accelerator. If the engine cannot stabilize at that low speed before the transmission engages neutral or shifts into park, the vehicle will shudder violently. Similarly, "fluttering" during takeoff suggests the engine is momentarily starving for air-fuel mixture or struggling to match wheel speed with gear ratios.

The most frequent culprit in vehicles of this generation is a dirty or failed Throttle Position Sensor (TPS) combined with carbon buildup on the throttle body. The TPS acts as the primary feedback loop for the Powertrain Control Module (PCM). When you lift your foot, the PCM expects a specific voltage drop corresponding to closed-throttle conditions. If the sensor provides erratic data due to wear or contamination, the PCM cannot accurately command the idle air control valve to adjust airflow. Consequently, the engine RPMs dip below the stability threshold, causing the drivetrain to jerk as the torque converter slips against the clutch packs in manual mode or simply stumbles before re-engaging.

To diagnose this systematically, start by inspecting the throttle body for excessive carbon deposits. A thick layer of black grime around the butterfly valve can prevent it from sealing completely or moving freely. Cleaning this component is a low-cost intervention that often resolves idle instability. Use a dedicated carburetor cleaner and a soft brush to remove buildup, ensuring the valve plate moves through its full range of motion without binding. After cleaning, you may need to perform an idle relearn procedure. This involves disconnecting the negative battery terminal for 30 seconds to reset adaptive fuel trims, or following a specific key-cycle sequence outlined in the service manual to allow the PCM to recalibrate the idle target RPM.

Another possibility is a vacuum leak upstream of the Throttle Body. If unmetered air enters the intake manifold, the air-fuel ratio leans out, causing the engine to run rough at low loads. Listen for hissing sounds near the brake booster hose or the PCV valve. A cracked vacuum line is a common failure point in 2012 model year Buicks. Replacing these lines restores the correct pressure differential required for smooth idle transitions.

If cleaning and reseating components does not resolve the issue, the problem may lie with the torque converter. The torque converter uses a lock-up clutch to mechanically connect the engine to the transmission at highway speeds. If this clutch fails to engage or disengage smoothly, you will feel a distinct shudder during acceleration and a jerk when coming to a stop. Diagnosis here requires checking transmission fluid levels and condition; dark, burnt-smelling fluid indicates internal degradation that likely necessitates a flush or replacement.

There is also the consideration of the electronic throttle body itself. In some cases, the motor inside the throttle body wears out, preventing it from returning to the exact closed position needed for a stable idle. This mechanical failure mimics a software error but requires physical replacement of the unit rather than just cleaning. Before replacing parts, verify that no diagnostic trouble codes (DTCs) are stored in the PCM via an OBD-II scanner. Codes like P0121 or P0505 often correlate directly with these symptoms and can guide whether the issue is sensor-related or actuator-related.

Ultimately, the goal is to ensure the engine maintains a stable idle speed before the transmission demands zero torque from the wheels. Whether it requires cleaning carbon deposits, replacing vacuum hoses, or swapping out the throttle body, addressing the root cause of the airflow instability will eliminate the jerking sensation and restore smooth drivability.
